All topics · Chess · Lesson 5

The double attack

One sitting (~35 minutes): a 10-minute reading, then about 25 minutes on the page. One win: you look for forks on purpose (targets first, then a square that hits two), for knights, queens and pawns, and you spot the ones aimed at you.

Why this lesson

In your 2 October game you were winning: after 30 moves Stockfish rated the position about +2.5 for you. Black had just played 30…exf3. You recaptured with 31. gxf3, and Black answered 31…Qe3+: one queen move that checked your king and attacked your rook on c1. Two moves later it was mate.

A single attack is easy to meet: move the piece, or guard it. A double attack (a fork when one piece does both jobs) gives your opponent two problems and only one move to solve them. Grandmaster Yuri Averbakh, quoted in the book's Chapter 1 (p. 6), goes as far as calling the double attack, in a broad sense, "the basis of most tactical operations", and Seirawan ends up agreeing.

Reading (about 10 minutes)

Reading

Seirawan & Silman, Winning Chess Tactics, Chapter 2 "The Double Attack":

  1. "Forks", from the bottom of p. 18 through "King Forks" on p. 21 (Diagrams 10–15). Mostly diagrams: set each one up in your head or on a board and find the fork before reading the answer.
  2. "Pawn Forks", p. 31 (Diagram 26 only).

Skip for now: "Discovered Attacks" (pp. 9–17; you met the idea in lesson 3) and the tests. "Forks as Combinations" (pp. 22–24) is optional: this page teaches the same idea with new positions.

Two things that read oddly: the book counts material in points (pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9), and it refers back to "Silman's Rules of Recognition" from Chapter 1 (p. 6): tactics need a weak (open) king, a king with no legal moves, an undefended piece, or a piece that isn't guarded enough. Forks feed mostly on the last three.

Hold these questions while you read; answer them in the boxes below.

Which pieces does the book show forking? Which one surprised you?

The book gives a fact about which squares a knight can attack at the same time (p. 19). What is it, and how could it help you?

What surprised or confused you in the reading?

Warm-up: what did their move do? (3 minutes)

Recap: the two steps from lesson 3

A move creates a new threat in only two ways: (1) the moved piece attacks something from its new square, or (2) the square it left opens a line for a piece behind it (a discovered attack). Then count attackers and defenders on anything attacked (lesson 1).

Run step 2: the black pawn left e4, so the e-file is open in front of Black's queen on e8. If the queen goes to e3 (with check), how many of your pieces does it attack from there, counting your king?

Two: the king on g1 (diagonal e3–f2–g1, so it's check) and the rook on c1 (diagonal e3–d2–c1). Nothing guards the rook, and the check means you have no time to save it. That's a fork. (Counted with python-chess.)

The idea, from something that's always true (from the reading, plus a routine)

Your opponent gets exactly one move before you move again.

So a single attack is easy to meet: one move saves the one piece. Two attacks at once win material unless one move answers both, and one move can do that in only a few ways. Check each before you call it a fork:

  • take the forking piece (is the fork square safe? count it, lesson 1),
  • answer with a check of their own, or
  • one move that saves both (moving one target so it guards the other, or one piece that guards both).

If none of those works, the fork wins material. That gives a routine you can always finish:

  1. Targets first. The enemy king, any piece nobody defends, and any piece worth more than your attacker (a knight forking a rook and a queen wins even if both are defended).
  2. A square that hits two. For each pair of targets, ask which of your pieces can reach, this move, a square that attacks both.
  3. Is the square safe? Count it, and run the three escapes above.

Step 1 is the one people skip. (That's my advice, and it matches Silman's Rules of Recognition: unguarded pieces and an open king are what make tactics possible.) You rarely find a fork by staring at your own pieces.

Knight forks (from the reading)

A knight jumps, so nothing blocks it, and it attacks up to eight squares. The book gives a quick filter on p. 19: the knight "can never attack squares of two different colors at the same time." The reason:

Every knight move goes to a square of the other colour. So a knight on a light square attacks only dark squares, and the other way round, and two targets on different colours can never be forked by one knight.

(Checked for all 64 squares with python-chess.) It's a filter, not a guarantee: two targets on the same colour still need a square that reaches both.

Step 1, targets. The king on g8, and the rook on e8: nothing guards it (the king doesn't reach e8 from g8, and the bishop on a6 is on the other diagonal).

Step 2, a square that hits both. g8 and e8 are both light squares, so a knight standing on a dark square might reach both. The square is f6: from f6 a knight attacks e8, g8, d7, h7, d5, h5, e4 and g4. Your knight on d5 can jump there.

Step 3, is f6 safe? Count it: no black pawn or piece attacks f6 (the g-pawn is on g6, not g7). No black check is possible, and no single black move saves both king and rook.

So 1. Nf6+ wins the rook: Black must move the king, then 2. Nxe8. Stockfish rates it about three points better than any other move. The book calls a fork of the king and the queen a royal fork; this one is king and rook.

White to move; material is level (no queens). Run the routine: targets first, then a square that hits two, then check it's safe. Find the move that wins material.

1. Nc7+ forks the king on e8 and the rook on a8, and nothing black guards c7. After the king moves, 2. Nxa8. Stockfish: best move by over two points.

White's 1. Nf6+ attacks the king on g8 and the rook on e8. Is it a good move here?

A black pawn on g7 attacks f6 (pawns capture diagonally forward), so 1. Nf6+ gxf6 just loses the knight. The king on g8 doesn't touch f6. This is the worked example's position with one change, the g-pawn on g7 instead of g6. Step 3 is why the routine has three steps: a fork on an unsafe square is a gift.

Black has a king on g8 and a queen on d8. On how many of the 64 squares could a white knight stand and attack both at once?

None. g8 is a light square and d8 is dark, and a knight's targets are always the same colour as each other (the opposite of its own square). From f6 or e7 a knight reaches g8 but not d8; from e6 it reaches d8 but not g8. (Counted over all 64 squares with python-chess.)

Queen forks (from the reading)

A queen moves like a rook and a bishop together, so it can hit targets in up to eight directions from one square. The usual queen fork is a check plus a loose piece: the check takes away the opponent's one move.

You've already played one. In your 6 October game:

Targets: White's king on h7 and the rook on d7, which nothing guards.

A square that hits both: f5 is on the diagonal f5–g6–h7 (check) and on the diagonal f5–e6–d7 (the rook). Two diagonals, one square.

Safe? Nothing white attacks f5, and White has no check. The king must move, and 60…Qxd7 followed. Stockfish found mate in five from here; you found the fork.

Built for this lesson, checked with Stockfish. White to move. Find the queen fork.

1. Qd5+: the diagonal d5–e6–f7–g8 checks the king, and the diagonal d5–c6–b7–a8 hits the rook. Black's queen on c7 can't cover a8. Black can only move the king or block with 1…Qf7, and either way 2. Qxa8+ follows. Stockfish's best move by a wide margin.

Pawn forks (from the reading)

A pawn attacks the two squares diagonally in front of it, so a pawn push can fork two pieces side by side. Because the pawn is worth less than either target, it doesn't matter whether the targets are defended: either one is worth more than the pawn. (Step 3 still applies to the square the pawn goes to: if they can take the pawn for free, the fork never happens.)

The book's example (Diagram 26, p. 31): Black plays 1…Bd6??, putting the bishop on d6, next to another black piece on f6.

Targets: two black pieces side by side on the 6th rank, each worth more than a pawn.

A square that hits both: e5, diagonally in front of both. White's pawn on e4 can step there: 2. e5!

Safe? Even if Black takes the pawn, a pawn for a piece is a good trade for White, and one move can't move both pieces. Black loses one.

Built for this lesson, checked with Stockfish. White to move. Find the pawn fork.

1. d5 attacks the knight on c6 and the bishop on e6. Taking it doesn't help: 1…Bxd5 2. Nxd5 and Black is still a piece down. Stockfish rates it best by more than three points.

Making a fork happen in two moves (beyond the reading; the book's pp. 22–24 if you read them)

Sometimes the fork square is guarded, or a target is on the wrong square. Then look for a forcing first move (a capture or a check) that removes the guard or drives a target onto the fork square.

Targets: the queen on e4. A knight on g5 would attack it, but it's just one target: the queen would step away.

Bring a second target into range: a knight on g5 also attacks f7. So put Black's king there: 1. Bxf7+!

If 1…Kxf7, then 2. Ng5+ forks the king on f7 and the queen on e4. The king must move, and 3. Nxe4.

If Black declines with 1…Kf8, 2. Bxe8 just wins a rook. If 1…Kh8, White has won a pawn, and 2. Re1 attacks the queen while the bishop on f7 attacks the rook on e8: another double attack, and Black can't fix both. Stockfish rates 1. Bxf7+ about five points better than any other move.

Built for this lesson, checked with Stockfish. White to move; material is level. A knight on e7 would fork the king on g8 and the queen on c6, but the rook on e8 guards e7. Find the first move that makes the fork work.

1. Rxe8+! Black must recapture, 1…Bxe8, and now nothing guards e7: 2. Ne7+ forks the king and the queen, then 3. Nxc6. Stockfish: nearly six points better than anything else.

Seeing their fork before it lands

Run the same routine for your opponent: your king and your loose pieces are the targets. Back to your 2 October game, the warm-up position:

Black threatens 31…Qe3+, which checks your king on g1 and attacks your rook on c1. Find a move that stops it and keeps your advantage.

31. Re7 (or 31. Qe7) blocks the e-file, so the queen can't reach e3. Stockfish keeps you about +2.5 after either one; every other move loses the advantage, and the game's 31. gxf3 lost to 31…Qe3+.

Take it to a real game

Play one game (any time control, the bot is fine). Before each of your moves, spend ten seconds on step 1 for both sides: where are the kings and the loose pieces? If two of theirs can be hit from one square, you may have a fork; if two of yours can, guard one or block the line. Send me the PGN and the review will check exactly this.

This is optional, and the next lesson works without it. Questions about anything here: ask me in chat.
